title: Views: Saving a Query Under a Name
what_is_it: A VIEW saves a SELECT query under a name so you can query it later like a table - CREATE VIEW defines one, CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW redefines it in place, and DROP VIEW removes it. Critically, a view is NOT a copy of the data: it re-runs its saved query every time you select from it, so it always reflects the CURRENT state of the underlying tables.
why_it_matters: Views are a readability and reuse tool - if several queries all need 'products priced above X' or 'departments with their headcount,' defining that once as a view means every caller gets the same, always-current logic instead of copy-pasting (and potentially drifting) the same SELECT everywhere.
output:
name       | price
-----------------+-------
 Mechanical Keyboard | 79.99
 Standing Mat        | 45.00
 USB-C Hub           | 34.50
common_mistakes: Expecting a view to be faster than just running its underlying query directly - it isn't, since a plain view has no storage of its own and re-executes the SELECT every time (that's what a MATERIALIZED VIEW is for, which does cache results). Also forgetting that DROP VIEW never touches the real table's data - it only removes the saved query.
mini_exercise: If products.price changes after you create a view over it, does querying that view again show the OLD price or the NEW one? Why?
postgres_note: Postgres also supports MATERIALIZED VIEW, which DOES store a snapshot of the result and must be explicitly refreshed (REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW) to pick up new data - useful for expensive queries you're willing to serve slightly stale.
